name: Dersimelagon

angle.text: Tanning-focused circles follow dersimelagon because it is an oral MC1R agonist that darkens skin pigment, in the way of melanocortin tanning peptides. It was developed for light-sensitivity disorders, so any use for a cosmetic tan is off-label, and no trials have looked at appearance.

summary: MT-7117, an investigational oral MC1R agonist that darkens skin pigment to protect people with light-sensitivity disorders; it is not a tanning product and has no looks-related trials.
note: Investigational drug studied for erythropoietic protoporphyria and systemic sclerosis; not approved as of the sources reviewed, and not studied for cosmetic tanning.
currentQuick:
Dersimelagon (MT-7117) is an experimental pill that switches on the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R), the receptor that drives skin pigment production. It is being developed for rare light-sensitivity diseases, mainly erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) and X-linked protoporphyria (XLP), and for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis [2][3][7].
It is covered here because it is a pigment-related compound, a non-peptide cousin of injectable tanning peptides. No study has looked at it as a cosmetic tan or for appearance in healthy people.
How it works: It is an orally available, non-peptide, selective MC1R agonist that increases skin eumelanin, the dark pigment [6][8]. In EPP and XLP, more pigment is intended to reduce painful reactions to visible light [6]. MC1R activation also has anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects in laboratory models, which is why it was studied in systemic sclerosis [9].
Risks and caveats: Its safety and efficacy are described by reviewers as needing further characterization [2]. Because it targets the pigment pathway, skin darkening is an expected pharmacological effect. It is investigational, so it has no consumer product or legal cosmetic status.
deepLead:
Dersimelagon (formerly MT-7117; developed as dersimelagon phosphoric acid) is an investigational, orally administered, nonpeptide small-molecule selective agonist of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) . Activation of MC1R drives melanogenesis in pigment cells and also has anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects .
It has been studied for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) and X-linked protoporphyria (XLP), rare disorders in which accumulating protoporphyrin causes painful phototoxic reactions to visible light, and for diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis . The only approved treatment for EPP at the time of recent reviews is afamelanotide, a peptide MC1R agonist given as a subcutaneous implant .
The compound is of interest to the wiki's pigment category rather than as a cosmetic product. No published study has tested it for tanning or appearance in healthy people, and it is not marketed.

name: Semax

angle.text: Semax is used in study-maxxing and nootropic circles for focus, learning and neuroprotection, not for appearance. Forum posters sometimes mention libido as a side benefit. Human evidence consists of small stroke trials in Russia, and no appearance effect has been studied.

summary: A Russian ACTH(4-10)-derived nootropic peptide with small stroke trials in Russia and a following in 'study-maxxing' circles; it has no studied effect on appearance.
note: Not an appearance compound; human data are mostly Russian-language stroke and neurology studies. Not FDA- or EMA-approved. Forum discussions often involve minors asking about use.
currentQuick:
Semax is a seven-amino-acid peptide (Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro) derived from a fragment of ACTH. It originates in Russian research and is reportedly used there for stroke and other neurological conditions [1][5][11]. It is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a focus and study aid rather than as a looks compound, and forum users disagree about whether it does anything [19][24][20].
Published work includes small, mostly Russian-language clinical studies in stroke and optic nerve disease, and many animal and cell studies [3][4][8]. No study has examined it for appearance.
How it works: In rats it raises brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor trkB in the hippocampus after intranasal application, and it alters gene expression after experimental stroke [9][10][12]. Imaging work has examined effects on brain network connectivity [13]. Human mechanisms are less well characterized.
Risks and caveats: Long-term safety data are limited outside Russia, and reviews of therapeutic peptides note a lack of clinical trials [2]. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA [1]. Users on forums frequently buy it from unregulated sources and some are teenagers asking about use [6][7].
deepLead:
Semax is a synthetic heptapeptide (Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro) that combines an ACTH(4-7) fragment with a Pro-Gly-Pro tail, giving a long-lasting analogue of ACTH(4-10) without hormonal activity . It was developed in Russia and is described in Russian literature as a nootropic and neuroprotective agent .
In published studies, it has been tested in patients with ischemic stroke, optic nerve disease and motor neuron disease , and in laboratory models of brain ischemia, where researchers report effects on neurotrophin and immune-related gene expression . A 2026 review of peptides in orthopaedics describes semax among neuroactive peptides and notes the lack of clinical trials for that field .
Semax is not an appearance compound. It appears in looksmaxxing spaces because the communities also discuss peptides, and users talk about it as a cognitive or study aid, with views ranging from enthusiastic to dismissive .

name: Hydroxypinacolone retinoate

chain: Fewer fine lines, more even tone
angle.text: HPR, sold as Granactive Retinoid, is used as a gentler cosmetic retinoid for fine lines and dark spots, often by people who find retinol irritating. Published human data are small and mostly come from combination products rather than HPR alone.

summary: HPR, sold as Granactive Retinoid, is a retinoic acid ester marketed as a gentler cosmetic retinoid; published human data are small and mostly use combination products.
note: Cosmetic ingredient, not a drug. Human studies are small and typically test mixtures (with retinol, peptides or acids), so HPR's own effect is hard to isolate.
currentQuick:
Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is an ester of retinoic acid used in over-the-counter skincare. Its best-known commercial form is Granactive Retinoid, a trademarked 10% HPR solution from Grant Industries [1]. It is marketed as a retinoid for lines and acne with less irritation than retinol or tretinoin.
Research is modest. Small Italian studies tested HPR-containing gels in acne, Chinese studies tested it in anti-aging serums, and laboratory work compares it with other retinoids. Most human studies use combination formulas, so conclusions about HPR alone are limited.
How it works: Manufacturer-derived descriptions say HPR can bind retinoid receptors directly without needing conversion, which is claimed to explain lower irritation [1]. Independent clinical comparisons with tretinoin are not reported in the studies reviewed. 
Risks and caveats: Trials of HPR-containing products report mild local effects such as dryness, peeling, erythema and burning in about 15% of participants in one open study [2]. A laboratory study found retinoid products often lose potency with storage and light [4]. Retinoic acid itself is banned in cosmetics because of safety concerns [11]. Pregnancy safety data for HPR were not found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is a synthetic retinoid ester that appears in cosmetic skincare, either on its own or alongside retinol or retinyl propionate . A 2021 stability study treated it as a newer retinoid in commercial cosmetics alongside retinol, retinyl palmitate and beta-carotene . It is sold under the trade name Granactive Retinoid, a trademarked mixture of 10% HPR in dimethyl isosorbide developed by Grant Industries, according to Grokipedia, which dates the product's introduction to late 2014 and says it was licensed to brands including The Ordinary .
Sources describe its chemistry slightly differently: a 2015 clinical paper calls it a synthetic ester of 9-cis-retinoic acid, whereas Grokipedia describes it as the pinacolyl ester of all-trans retinoic acid . Marketing materials describe it as binding retinoid receptors directly and as less irritating than retinol .
Evidence on HPR in people consists of small open or comparative studies, most using combination products for acne or photoaging, plus in-vitro and zebrafish work .

name: Retinaldehyde (Retinal)

chain: Converts to retinoic acid in skin
angle.text: Retinal is used in over-the-counter serums as a middle step between retinol and prescription tretinoin, for wrinkles and uneven tone. Skin-specific human evidence is sparse, with most studies being older or still registered.

summary: The vitamin A form one step before retinoic acid, sold in OTC serums as a middle-ground retinoid; skin-specific human evidence is sparse and mostly old or still registered.
note: Do not confuse with the retina (eye anatomy), which dominates search results. Skin trials are few and small.
currentQuick:
Retinaldehyde (retinal) is the aldehyde form of vitamin A. In the body, it is part of the pathway that converts retinol into retinoic acid, the active form that tretinoin supplies directly [1]. It is also the light-sensing chromophore in vision, which is what most of the biological literature about it concerns [1].
In skincare it is sold as an over-the-counter retinoid positioned between retinol and prescription tretinoin. Published skin studies are few: an exploratory 1999 trial in rosacea, a 1999 human tolerance study, and a registered split-face study in aging skin [2][3][4].
How it works: Retinal is described as a precursor to retinoic acid, which acts through retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and retinoid X receptors to influence gene expression, cell differentiation and epithelial maintenance [1]. The 1999 rosacea trial described retinaldehyde as a retinoic acid precursor [2].
Risks and caveats: The 1999 trial of topical retinaldehyde in humans specifically assessed tolerance, but its results are not summarized in the source reviewed [3]. No published data in the sources reviewed quantify irritation or other adverse effects for retinaldehyde on skin. Retinal is chemically reactive and oxidizes readily, according to Grokipedia [1].
deepLead:
Retinaldehyde, usually shortened to retinal, is the aldehyde form of vitamin A (retinol) with the formula C20H28O . In biology it is best known as the chromophore of vertebrate vision, where its 11-cis isomer binds opsin proteins, and as an intermediate that can be converted onward to retinoic acid . In cosmetic skincare, it is sold as a retinoid said to sit between retinol and tretinoin in strength.
Skin-focused evidence is thin. A 1999 exploratory clinical study applied a 0.05% retinaldehyde cream daily for 6 months to women with vascular signs of facial rosacea, and a companion 1999 randomized study examined its tolerance in humans . A split-face study of stabilized retinaldehyde in aging skin (56 participants) is registered as completed .
In looksmaxxing forums, retinal appears as a lower-strength option that some users alternate with stronger prescription retinoids while skin adjusts .

name: Trifarotene (Aklief)

chain: Clearer skin on face and trunk
angle.text: Aklief is a prescription retinoid cream used for acne on the face, chest and back, and users discuss it as a step before isotretinoin. Its acne use is studied in large vehicle-controlled trials and is FDA-approved; no anti-aging approval exists.

summary: Aklief is an Rx RAR-gamma-selective retinoid cream approved in 2019 for acne on the face and trunk; large vehicle-controlled trials back it, and no anti-aging approval exists.
note: Prescription-only. Irritation, dryness and sunburn are the most common adverse reactions; pregnancy data are limited.
currentQuick:
Trifarotene (Aklief) is a prescription topical retinoid from Galderma, approved by the US FDA in October 2019 for acne vulgaris in people aged 9 and older [2][3]. It is described as a first-in-class, fourth-generation retinoid that selectively targets the retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma) [2][6].
Its main distinction is that the pivotal studies enrolled people with acne on both the face and the trunk, giving it rigorous clinical data on truncal acne that other topical retinoids lack [4][6]. Later phase 4 trials have looked at post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and atrophic acne scars [9][11].
How it works: Trifarotene is an agonist of retinoic acid receptors with particular activity at the gamma subtype, the most common isoform in skin [3][6]. Like other topical retinoids, it increases keratinocyte differentiation and reduces proliferation, which lowers hyperkeratinization, and may reduce inflammation [6]. The label states that the exact process by which it improves acne is unknown [3].
Risks and caveats: The most common adverse reactions (1% or more) are application-site irritation, itching and sunburn [3]. The label advises moisturizer, reduced frequency if needed, and sun protection [3]. Available trial data have not identified a pregnancy-related risk, but case reports with other topical retinoids describe birth defects similar to those from oral retinoids [3].
deepLead:
Trifarotene, sold as Aklief (a 0.005% cream), is a topical retinoid developed by Galderma that selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma) and is classed as a fourth-generation retinoid . The US FDA approved it in October 2019 for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 9 years of age and older .
Its distinguishing feature is clinical data on truncal acne. Reviewers state that, unlike earlier topical retinoids, it is the first with rigorous trial data on safety and efficacy for acne on the trunk as well as the face . It is approved for acne only; it does not carry an anti-aging indication, and Grokipedia notes limited clinical evidence for anti-aging use .
In looksmaxxing forums, trifarotene appears mostly as a prescription step between tretinoin and isotretinoin for acne, discussed by teenagers and young adults .

name: Retinyl palmitate

chain: Converted to retinol, then retinoic acid
angle.text: Retinyl palmitate is the vitamin A ester found in moisturisers and sunscreens, and some users treat it as the gentlest retinoid for skin aging. It is the least-studied cosmetic retinoid for wrinkles, and its use on sun-exposed skin has been debated for years.

summary: A storage-form vitamin A ester found in moisturisers, sunscreens and supplements; the weakest-studied cosmetic retinoid, with a long-running safety debate over its use on sun-exposed skin.
note: Reviews say cosmetic retinoids are not required to show clinical efficacy; a mouse photocarcinogenicity study led to debate that regulatory panels did not translate into a human-use limit below 3%.
currentQuick:
Retinyl palmitate is the ester of retinol (vitamin A) with palmitic acid [1]. It is common in over-the-counter skincare, fortified foods and supplements, and is a stable, fat-soluble precursor that the body or skin must convert into active retinoids [1]. Reviews of cosmetic retinoids place it among the first-generation retinoids used in cosmeceuticals, alongside retinol and retinaldehyde [2].
The evidence for its skin benefits is thinner than for tretinoin. A review notes that cosmetic retinoids such as retinol, retinaldehyde and retinyl palmitate are marketed as cosmetics, which do not require clinical efficacy studies, raising concerns about their efficacy [3]. A separate review concluded that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated [2].
How it works: In the skin, retinyl esters are thought to be hydrolysed to retinol and converted stepwise to retinoic acid, which acts on retinoid receptors [1][2]. Reviews note that retinoids in cosmetics face problems of instability, low penetration and irritation [3].
Risks and caveats: A US National Toxicology Program study in mice reported faster tumour development when retinyl palmitate was applied with simulated sunlight; the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel judged it safe in cosmetics up to 3%, and a European committee found no phototoxic potential, according to Grokipedia [1]. High-dose supplement trials such as CARET gave retinyl palmitate with beta-carotene to smokers and asbestos-exposed workers [6]. The injectable medical form carries warnings about overdose and anaphylaxis [7].
deepLead:
Retinyl palmitate is an ester formed between retinol (vitamin A) and palmitic acid (formula C36H60O2), used in cosmetics, fortified foods and dietary supplements as a stable source of vitamin A . In skincare it is grouped among the first-generation retinoids, which also include all-trans retinoic acid, retinol and retinaldehyde, although it is not itself the active form and must be converted in tissue .
Evidence for cosmetic benefit comes mainly from reviews rather than trials of retinyl palmitate on its own. One 2025 review of cosmetic retinoids in photoaging concluded that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde used in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated, with all-trans retinoic acid regarded as the gold standard . A 2022 review says efficacy concerns exist because clinical studies are not required to market cosmetics, and that retinoids pose formulation challenges (instability, low penetration, irritation) .
The compound is also the subject of a public safety controversy over its use in sunscreens and day creams, based on a mouse photocarcinogenicity study. Regulatory and expert panels cited in Grokipedia concluded that it is safe in cosmetics at concentrations up to 3% . In forums it appears in talk of vitamin A intake and as an ingredient some users say they avoid .

name: Poly-L-lactic acid (Sculptra)

chain: Fuller cheeks, softer folds, defined contours
angle.text: Sculptra is injected to restore cheek and midface volume, soften cheek lines, and rebuild a gaunt face after weight loss, with results building gradually over weeks. Randomized trials and systematic reviews report effects lasting up to about two years.

summary: Sculptra, an injectable PLLA collagen stimulator for midface volume and cheek lines; randomized trials and systematic reviews show effects lasting up to about two years, with nodules a known risk.
note: Clinician-administered injectable; results build over several sessions. Nodules, bruising and swelling are the reported adverse effects, and rare serious events have been described.
currentQuick:
Sculptra is a Galderma injectable whose active ingredient is poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a biodegradable synthetic polymer [1][4]. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, which add immediate volume, PLLA is classed as a collagen biostimulator: it is injected to prompt the body to lay down collagen gradually, restoring facial volume and smoothing wrinkles over time [1][4].
It was first approved by the US FDA in 2004 for facial fat loss in people with HIV, and its indications later expanded to nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles, according to Grokipedia [1]. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report improved skin elasticity, wrinkle reduction and facial volume, with effects sustained for up to 25 months [2][3].
How it works: PLLA microparticles are described as promoting a subclinical inflammatory response that leads to collagen deposition in the extracellular matrix, so volume is restored gradually rather than immediately [4]. A 2025 gene analysis in a randomized comparison reported that PLLA triggered regeneration-related gene activity, whereas calcium hydroxylapatite induced inflammation-related activity [7].
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse events across trials are mostly mild to moderate: bruising, hematoma, tenderness, nodules and swelling [3]. A 2026 systematic review found mild injection-site pain and swelling as the most frequent effects and reported at least one serious case [2]. It is injected by trained clinicians. Poor technique or product selection can cause lumps, which reviewers list among the main adverse events [3].
deepLead:
Sculptra is a brand of injectable poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), a synthetic, biocompatible and biodegradable polymer, marketed by Galderma as a collagen-stimulating dermal treatment . It is used to restore volume in the cheeks and midface, to soften nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles, and, in its original indication, to correct facial lipoatrophy in HIV .
Unlike conventional hyaluronic acid fillers, PLLA is described as a biostimulator: its microparticles are said to provoke a controlled subclinical inflammatory response that lays down collagen, so results emerge over weeks to months and typically involve several treatment sessions . Systematic reviews of randomized trials report improvements in skin quality, volume and lipoatrophy scores, with benefits sustained up to 25 months, and adverse events that are mostly mild to moderate .
In looksmaxxing communities, it is discussed mainly as an option for a gaunt face after weight loss; the community material is limited to a few forum questions .

name: Deoxycholic acid (Kybella)

angle.text: Kybella is an injectable approved for reducing a double chin, used to sharpen the jaw and neck line without surgery. Fat removal in the treated area is visible once swelling settles, and some users also ask about other small fat pads.

summary: Injectable fat-cell destroyer approved for double chins; works on a small area, with swelling and rare nerve injury.
note: Approved only for submental fat; marginal mandibular nerve injury and dysphagia are labelled warnings.
currentQuick:
Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid that the body makes to digest fat. A synthetic version, sold as Kybella, is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells and reduce a double chin. The US FDA approved it in 2015 for adults with moderate to severe submental fullness.
People in looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a lower-downtime alternative to liposuction for the chin and neck, and sometimes ask about using it elsewhere on the face. Off-label use is not recommended on the label and has been tested only in small studies.
How it works: Injected into fat under the skin, the drug acts as a detergent that disrupts fat-cell membranes so the cells burst. The body then clears the debris over several months.
Risks and caveats: The label lists swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, redness and hardness as the most common reactions. Warnings include injury to the facial nerve branch controlling the lower lip, trouble swallowing and hair loss in the treated area. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid, produced when gut bacteria modify cholic acid, that normally helps emulsify dietary fats . A synthetic, injectable form is sold in the United States as Kybella and elsewhere as Belkyra. It is a prescription cytolytic drug that is injected under the skin to destroy fat cells, and it is approved for improving the appearance of moderate to severe convexity or fullness caused by submental fat (a "double chin") in adults .
The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in April 2015 . The product was developed as ATX-101 by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals . Its label states that it is not approved for subcutaneous fat outside the submental region and that such use is not recommended . Researchers have nonetheless registered or published small studies of off-label areas such as the jowls, upper inner thigh, flanks and bra-strap region .
In looksmaxxing communities it appears mainly as an alternative to liposuction for a recessed-looking jawline or neck, and men on looksmax.org have posted about having it done . The label's reported adverse effects include swelling, bruising, pain, numbness and, less often, injury to the facial nerve branch that moves the lower lip .

name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler

chain: Lasting volume in chin, cheeks, scars
angle.text: PMMA filler (Artefill, Bellafill) is injected for permanent volume in the cheeks and chin and to lift acne scars, so the result is visible straight away and stays. Outcome data are limited, and bodybuilders have also injected PMMA-type products for muscle size.

summary: Permanent filler beads that stay in the face for good; few sources on outcomes, and removal is difficult if problems arise.
note: Permanent: the FDA says removal can be difficult or impossible; granulomas and migration can appear years later.
currentQuick:
PMMA filler is made of tiny plastic beads in a gel. The beads are not absorbed, so the body forms tissue around them and the effect is considered permanent. In the US, permanent fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.
In forums it comes up mostly as a warning: users ask about it when a surgeon offers PMMA bone cement for implants, and bodybuilding forums mention it in connection with muscle-shaping injections.
How it works: The microspheres act as a scaffold that the body cannot break down; surrounding tissue forms fibrous collagen around them, which adds volume.
Risks and caveats: The FDA lists lumps, granulomas, infection, migration, permanent hard nodules and rare vascular injury (including blindness) as possible filler complications, some appearing years later. Removal can be difficult or impossible. Use in the buttocks, muscles or other unapproved sites is not sanctioned.
deepLead:
Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler is a non-absorbable injectable made of tiny PMMA microspheres suspended in a carrier gel, sold in the United States under names such as Artefill and Bellafill. Because the microspheres are not broken down by the body, the fillers are described as permanent: the particles stay in place and prompt the body to form fibrous tissue around them .
The US FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and for acne scars of the cheek, and it states that removal can be difficult or impossible for permanent fillers. A review of jawline and chin fillers includes PMMA among the materials used in the lower face . PMMA is the same polymer used in bone cement, dentures and other implants, and some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it to shape muscles .
Published human evidence on cosmetic PMMA filler in the sources used here is limited to registered studies and reviews. Looksmaxxing forums discuss PMMA mostly as a cautionary subject, for example when a surgeon offered PMMA bone cement for facial implants .

name: Poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA)

angle.text: PDLLA is a collagen-stimulating injectable used for skin quality, wrinkles and acne scar texture, related to PLLA. Improvements build up gradually over weeks. A handful of trials exist, and nodules are the main known risk.

summary: Collagen-stimulating injectable polymer related to PLLA; a handful of trials, nodules are the main known risk.
note: Nodules and granulomas are recognised complications; evidence is mostly small trials and reviews.
currentQuick:
PDLLA is a dissolvable polymer injected into skin to trigger the body to make new collagen, rather than just to plump a spot. It is used for wrinkles, nasolabial folds, scars and skin quality, and sits alongside PLLA and calcium hydroxylapatite in the biostimulator category.
Published support consists of a few randomised and open-label trials plus reviews; forum discussion appears to be minimal.
How it works: As the particles break down into lactic acid, the body mounts a mild inflammatory response and fibroblasts lay down collagen over weeks to months.
Risks and caveats: Reviews highlight granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules, which may need treatment such as triamcinolone. As with other fillers, the FDA notes some complications appear long after injection and that rare vascular events can occur.
deepLead:
Poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) is a biodegradable synthetic polymer used in injectable skin products classed as biostimulators. Rather than simply filling a space, biostimulatory fillers such as PDLLA, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), polycaprolactone and calcium hydroxylapatite are described as prompting a controlled inflammatory response that leads the body to produce new collagen .
Reviews describe PDLLA as improving skin elasticity and firmness, reducing wrinkles and supporting tissue regeneration and scar remodelling, while noting that granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules are recognised complications . One commercial product, AestheFill (REGEN Biotech, South Korea), has been compared with hyaluronic acid in a randomised nasolabial fold trial . PDLLA is also used in non-cosmetic settings such as bone fixation screws and drug-delivery particles, which are separate from the injectable use .
The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of PDLLA, and the published cosmetic evidence is a small set of trials and reviews.

name: Collagen filler

angle.text: Collagen filler is the original injectable, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add lip volume, with the plumping visible right after treatment. It is temporary, bovine versions can provoke allergies, and hyaluronic acid has largely replaced it.

summary: The original injectable filler; temporary and allergy-prone in bovine form, now largely overtaken by hyaluronic acid.
note: Bovine products can trigger hypersensitivity reactions; correction is temporary.
currentQuick:
Collagen fillers are injected into the skin to smooth lines and add volume. Bovine collagen (Zyderm, Zyplast) was the leading filler in the US for about two decades and was long treated as the gold standard before hyaluronic acid products took over.
The effect is temporary. Forums rarely discuss collagen injections today, and mentions of collagen mostly concern supplements.
How it works: The injected collagen physically adds volume under a wrinkle or fold and is gradually absorbed by the body.
Risks and caveats: Reviews note hypersensitivity reactions with bovine collagen, and the FDA advises allergy screening for fillers containing collagen. As with all fillers, bruising, swelling and lumps can occur; results are temporary.
deepLead:
Collagen fillers are injectable implants made from animal-derived or human bioengineered collagen, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add soft-tissue volume. They are generally regarded as the original modern injectable dermal filler: a 2006 review notes that bovine collagen was the most popular injectable implant in the United States for nearly two decades before human bioengineered collagen products and hyaluronic acid fillers became available .
A 2001 review described injectable Zyderm bovine collagen as having come to be regarded as the gold standard against which other fillers were measured . The correction is temporary, and bovine products can cause hypersensitivity reactions, which was the context for a randomised trial comparing hyaluronic acid (Restylane) with bovine collagen (Zyplast) in the nasolabial folds .
Collagen fillers have since been largely displaced in many markets by hyaluronic acid, though newer collagen-based and recombinant-collagen products continue to be registered for study . The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of collagen injections as a filler; forum mentions of collagen concern dietary supplements.

name: Polyacrylamide gel

angle.text: Polyacrylamide gel is a permanent injectable that has been used for facial contouring and for HIV-related facial fat loss, with volume visible once placed. Published cosmetic evidence is thin in the sources reviewed, and removal can be difficult.

summary: A permanent synthetic gel filler with little published cosmetic evidence in these sources; removal can be difficult.
note: Permanent fillers can be hard to remove; concerns centre on residual acrylamide monomer.
currentQuick:
Polyacrylamide gel is a water-rich synthetic gel that has been injected as a permanent filler for facial contouring and fat loss, and is also used in medicine for incontinence and, experimentally, knee osteoarthritis.
The sources contain few studies of its cosmetic use and no forum discussion. Evidence in other uses does not establish how it performs as a face filler.
How it works: The gel stays in place and adds volume as a non-absorbable bulking material.
Risks and caveats: Polyacrylamide is described as low in toxicity, but the acrylamide monomer is a neurotoxin and carcinogen, and contamination is a stated concern. The FDA says permanent fillers can cause nodules, migration and late complications and can be difficult or impossible to remove.
deepLead:
Polyacrylamide gel, in its injectable medical form polyacrylamide hydrogel (PAAG), is a water-based synthetic gel made of cross-linked polyacrylamide. It has been used as a permanent soft-tissue filler, including for facial contouring and for HIV-related facial fat loss, and the same type of material is used in other medical settings such as injections for urinary incontinence and, in a Danish trial, intra-articular injection for knee osteoarthritis .
Polyacrylamide itself is described as low in toxicity, but its precursor, the acrylamide monomer, is a recognised neurotoxin and carcinogen, and safety concerns about PAAG products have centred on possible residual monomer . The FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and says removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible.
One registered study follows 240 women who had polyacrylamide hydrogel removed from the breast and were reconstructed, which indicates that the material has been used for breast augmentation and has needed removal in some patients . The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of PAAG as a facial filler.

name: Mercury skin lightening

angle.text: Mercury-containing creams and soaps are used in informal markets to pale skin and fade dark spots. Mercury salts do inhibit melanin production. They are banned in many countries and have no clinical cosmetic use.

summary: Toxic mercury-salt lightening creams banned in many countries but still found in informal markets; no clinical use.
note: WHO describes mercury lightening products as hazardous; kidney and neurological damage are reported.
currentQuick:
Some skin-lightening creams and soaps contain mercury salts, which pale the skin by suppressing melanin. They have a long history, from ancient Rome to the 19th century, and remain sold in informal and online markets despite bans in many countries.
There are no clinical trials of mercury as a cosmetic treatment and no forum discussion in the sources reviewed; the literature is about toxicity.
How it works: Inorganic mercury inhibits melanin production and accumulates in the skin, which also can discolour it over time.
Risks and caveats: WHO describes these products as hazardous: kidney damage, tremor, insomnia, memory loss and headaches have been reported, and some products contain undeclared mercury. A 2023 Minamata Convention amendment bars manufacture, import and export of mercury-added cosmetics after 2025.
deepLead:
Mercury skin lightening refers to the use of creams, soaps and lotions containing mercury compounds to make the skin paler or to fade dark spots. The World Health Organization describes skin lightening as a dangerous practice often associated with exposure to mercury salts, which inhibit melanin production, and says mercury-containing lightening products are hazardous and have been banned in many countries .
Mercury and lead compounds have a long history in cosmetics: Wikipedia reports mercury was used as a lightening agent in ancient Greece and Rome, and that white women in 19th-century America used products containing toxic amounts of lead and mercury . Today such products are still reported to be obtainable online and through informal channels, and some have been found to contain mercury without listing it as an ingredient .
Reported health effects of mercury exposure include kidney and neurological damage; it is not a treatment used in clinical dermatology. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of mercury creams, and no clinical trials of mercury lightening exist among them.

name: Clobetasol propionate

angle.text: Clobetasol is a prescription steroid for conditions such as psoriasis and eczema. It appears as a hidden ingredient in illicit lightening creams, where lightening is a side effect of its action on skin. Its use for lightening is off-label and unstudied.

summary: A super-potent prescription steroid that turns up in illicit lightening creams; its documented skin harms are significant.
note: Not approved for lightening; label limits use to 2 weeks and 50 g a week due to adrenal suppression.
currentQuick:
Clobetasol propionate is the strongest class of topical corticosteroid, prescribed for psoriasis, eczema, lichen conditions and similar. It is also reported as an ingredient in illicit skin-lightening creams, which is not an approved use.
No trials have tested it for lightening, and the sources contain no forum discussion of it.
How it works: It activates glucocorticoid receptors in the skin, dampening inflammation.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include skin thinning, bruising, visible capillaries, stretch marks, acne, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and adrenal suppression; Cushing's syndrome has been reported. The label limits use to two weeks and 50 g per week, and it is prescription-only in the US.
deepLead:
Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid, the top group in the seven-class US potency ranking . It is prescribed for corticosteroid-responsive skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, and as a treatment for cutaneous graft-versus-host disease .
Its relevance to appearance is as an undeclared or illicit ingredient in skin-lightening creams. Wikipedia reports that it is used cosmetically for skin whitening, that the FDA has not approved it for that purpose, and that products containing it are sold internationally and online, in some cases at higher concentrations than prescription products allow . A 2016 study cited there ranks it, with mercury and hydroquinone, among the most toxic and most-used lightening agents .
The US label restricts use to short courses and a maximum weekly amount because the drug can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis . No clinical trials have tested clobetasol as a skin-lightening treatment; its documented trial evidence concerns inflammatory skin disease. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of it.

name: Decapeptide-12

angle.text: Decapeptide-12 is a cosmetic peptide marketed for brightening and fading hyperpigmentation, with users comparing it to hydroquinone. Evidence consists of small, uncontrolled studies, often on multi-ingredient products, and skin penetration is a known limit.

summary: A cosmetic brightening peptide with only small, uncontrolled, multi-product studies behind it.
note: Studies tested it inside a system with glycolic acid and sunscreen, so its own effect is unclear.
currentQuick:
Decapeptide-12 is a short peptide sold in cosmetic brightening products for dark spots, melasma and sun-related pigmentation. Small open-label studies report improvement in melasma scores and photodamage grades.
Those studies used a full routine including glycolic acid and sunscreen and had no control group.
How it works: It is described as inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to reduce melanin content. Its size and water solubility limit how well it penetrates skin.
Risks and caveats: The open-label studies reported good tolerability and no adverse events in the small groups tested. Long-term safety data and independent controlled trials were not found in the sources used here.
deepLead:
Decapeptide-12 is a ten-amino-acid cosmetic peptide marketed for skin brightening. It is described in the literature as a novel peptide used to lighten hyperpigmentation, and a 2021 pharmaceutics paper characterises it as safer than hydroquinone in reducing melanin content, with efficacy of more than 50% over 16 weeks of twice-daily treatment, but limited by poor skin penetration because it is hydrophilic and large .
The human evidence consists of small open-label studies in which it was combined with other products rather than tested alone: a 0.01% decapeptide-12 cream used with an antioxidant cleanser, a glycolic-acid moisturiser or lotion and a broad-spectrum sunscreen . No controlled trial isolating the peptide is present among the sources used here.
The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of it.

name: Rice water

chain: Starch and amino acids on skin
angle.text: Rice water is a folk beauty rinse from parts of Asia, used on hair and as a skin wash for glow and an even tone. It is popular in beauty communities, and no trials have tested it for hair or skin.

summary: Starchy rice-rinse water used as a hair and skin wash in Asian folk beauty; popular, but no trials test it for hair or skin.
note: Evidence is anecdotal; arsenic content of rice and spoilage are noted concerns, mainly for internal use.
currentQuick:
Rice water is the milky liquid left over when rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled. It has long been used in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, and fermented versions are popular on social media.
Proponents say it makes hair shinier, stronger and less prone to breakage, and that it brightens and soothes skin. A review of social-media hair remedies examined the evidence behind such claims, and an encyclopedic overview describes studies of rice water itself as limited, with hair growth claims resting largely on anecdote.
How it works: Rice water contains starch plus small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids. Proponents point to compounds such as inositol and ferulic acid as the reason it might smooth hair strands, reduce friction and support skin, but this mechanism has not been shown in controlled human studies of rice water.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is generally treated as low risk, but no controlled safety data exist. Rice can contain arsenic, which is discussed mainly for drinking rice water, and prepared rice water can spoil if stored for long.
deepLead:
Rice water is the cloudy, starchy liquid left after rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled. It carries starch along with small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids leached from the grain, and it can also be left to ferment for a day or two before use. It has a long history of folk use in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, and it is also used as an oral fluid for diarrhoea.
In appearance-focused circles it is mainly promoted as a hair rinse for length, shine and reduced breakage, and as a skin toner said to soothe and brighten the complexion. A 2023 review of topical hair-loss remedies popular on TikTok, which included rice water alongside rosemary oil, onion juice and garlic gel, set out to examine the research behind such claims. An encyclopedic overview notes that studies of rice water itself are limited and that claims about faster hair growth rest mainly on anecdote, such as accounts from Yao women in China.
No clinical trial of rice water as a cosmetic skin or hair treatment appears in the sources reviewed. Related work exists on other rice-derived products, but it does not test rice water itself.

name: Turmeric (topical)

chain: Believed to calm and fade blemishes
angle.text: Turmeric pastes and masks are a long-standing South Asian preparation, promoted in appearance communities for brightening and evening skin tone and fading blemishes. One small vitiligo trial exists, none address cosmetic lightening, and the pigment can stain skin.

summary: Traditional yellow spice paste used for brightening; one small vitiligo trial exists, none for cosmetic lightening, and it stains.
note: Stains skin yellow; the only pigment-related trial is a pilot in vitiligo.
currentQuick:
Topical turmeric means applying turmeric root or its pigment curcumin to the skin, usually as a paste or cream. It is a traditional brightening and blemish remedy, especially in South Asia.
The human research is thin. One randomised pilot trial tested a turmeric cream in vitiligo, and other trials of curcumin products cover unrelated conditions. No trial of cosmetic skin lightening was found.
How it works: Curcumin has been studied for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-proliferative activity, which is the usual rationale for use. Whether this alters pigmentation in healthy skin has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Turmeric stains skin and fabric yellow. Yellow discolouration has been reported with oral supplements. Controlled safety data for topical cosmetic use are lacking.
deepLead:
Topical turmeric refers to the use of turmeric root (Curcuma longa) or its main pigment curcumin on the skin, as a paste, mask or cream. It is a long-standing household and traditional preparation in South Asia, promoted in appearance communities as a brightening, evening and anti-blemish ingredient.
Published human research on topical turmeric for skin appearance is sparse. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study tested a turmeric cream in vitiligo, a condition of pigment loss, and reported in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology in 2022. That study concerns a medical skin condition rather than general brightening, and no trial of turmeric for skin lightening in healthy skin appears in the sources reviewed.
Turmeric is a strong yellow dye. Case literature documents yellow skin discolouration after oral turmeric supplements, and the pigment's staining effect is a recognised practical feature of its topical use.

name: Powdered pearl

angle.text: Powdered pearl has about two thousand years of use in Chinese medicine for a luminous complexion, applied as a mask or taken by mouth. Research covers wound and bone repair, and its use for skin brightening is based on tradition.

summary: Ground pearl used in Chinese medicine for a luminous complexion; research covers wound and bone repair, not skin brightening.
note: No human trials for skin brightening; long-term safety data are limited.
currentQuick:
Powdered pearl is finely ground pearl or mother-of-pearl, a traditional Chinese medicine used for over two thousand years in beauty and health preparations. It is sold as a topical mask ingredient and as an oral powder.
Modern research mostly covers wound healing and bone repair in laboratory and animal models, with a few small human studies on other outcomes. No trial tests it for complexion or skin brightening.
How it works: Pearl is mostly calcium carbonate with a protein matrix. Researchers attribute antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair activity mainly to the water-soluble matrix proteins, studied in cells and animals.
Risks and caveats: Reviews say direct evidence on long-term safety, heavy-metal content and immune effects is limited. No safety data specific to cosmetic use appear in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Powdered pearl, or pearl powder, is finely ground pearl or nacre (mother-of-pearl), composed mainly of calcium carbonate with an organic protein matrix. It is a traditional Chinese medicine ingredient used for roughly two thousand years, and it is applied to the skin or taken by mouth for complexion and general health.
In appearance contexts it is promoted as a skin-brightening and anti-ageing ingredient. Published research is mostly laboratory, animal and biomaterials work on wound healing and bone repair, plus a few small human studies of other outcomes; a narrative review describes the evidence base as lacking in-depth understanding despite the long history of use. No trial of pearl powder for complexion or skin lightening appears in the sources reviewed.

name: Trenbolone

angle.text: Trenbolone is a veterinary steroid used by bodybuilders for muscle mass, strength and a lean, hard look. Forum posters also claim effects on height and facial structure. There are no human trials, and reviews of users report adverse effects in most.

summary: A potent veterinary-origin steroid used for a dry, hard physique; no human trials, and reviews report adverse effects in most users.
note: Not approved for humans; controlled in the US and banned in sport; contaminated products reported.
currentQuick:
Trenbolone is a synthetic steroid used in cattle to promote muscle growth. It has no human approval, but bodybuilders and some looksmaxxers use it to gain muscle and get a lean, vascular look.
No controlled human trials of its effect on muscle or appearance were found. What exists is mostly reviews of side effects and veterinary work. Forum claims that it helps bone growth or height are untested.
How it works: It binds the androgen receptor strongly, reportedly more so than testosterone, and is not converted to oestrogen. Anabolic effects in muscle are inferred from animal work and user reports rather than human trials.
Risks and caveats: A 2024 review reports adverse effects in about 90 percent of users, including acne, gynaecomastia, hypertension, arrhythmia, psychiatric effects and injection-site damage. It is a controlled substance in the US and prohibited in sport.
deepLead:
Trenbolone, often called tren, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) of the nandrolone group. It is used in veterinary medicine as a growth promoter in cattle, usually as the acetate ester in implants, and it has never been approved for human medical use. It is used non-medically by bodybuilders and other athletes who want more muscle mass, strength and a lean, vascular look.
Its pharmacology is described as a potent androgen receptor agonist with strong anabolic activity and little conversion to oestrogen. Published human research on trenbolone is almost entirely limited to reviews of adverse effects and to veterinary and environmental studies; no controlled human trial of its effect on muscle or appearance appears in the sources reviewed. A 2024 review concluded that trenbolone, like other AAS, is associated with frequent harmful effects, reporting that about 90 percent of users experience adverse effects.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed both as a physique drug and, among very young users, as a supposed aid to bone growth, a claim for which no supporting studies were found.

name: Nandrolone

chain: Greater lean mass and joint comfort
angle.text: Nandrolone (Deca) is an injectable steroid used by lifters for muscle size and, per forum claims, bone growth and joint comfort. Trials show lean-mass gains in patients with illness, and none exist in healthy lifters.

summary: A prescription-origin injectable steroid used for muscle; trials show lean-mass effects in sick patients, but none in healthy lifters.
note: Controlled substance and banned in sport; suppresses natural testosterone production; height claims untested.
currentQuick:
Nandrolone is an injectable anabolic steroid, best known as nandrolone decanoate (Deca-Durabolin). It has been prescribed for wasting, anaemia and osteoporosis, and is used by bodybuilders for muscle gain.
Trials in patients show effects on lean mass and related outcomes. No controlled trials in healthy people for appearance were found. Looksmaxxing posts promote it as hair-friendly and as a possible bone aid; the latter is untested.
How it works: It activates the androgen receptor and, unlike testosterone, is converted to a weaker androgen (DHN) rather than DHT. It also has progestogenic activity.
Risks and caveats: Reviews of illicit use report adverse effects across several organ systems, and cardiac deaths have been reported in AAS users generally. It suppresses natural testosterone production, is a US Schedule III drug, and is prohibited in sport.
deepLead:
Nandrolone, also called 19-nortestosterone, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) derived from testosterone by removal of one methyl group, and it is the parent compound of the 19-nor AAS subclass. It is usually given as an injectable ester, most often nandrolone decanoate (brand name Deca-Durabolin).
Medically it has been used for catabolic and wasting conditions such as anaemia of chronic kidney disease, osteoporosis, and tissue loss in HIV and burn patients. Outside medicine it is used by bodybuilders and other athletes for muscle size, strength and recovery, usually at higher doses than therapeutic ones. A systematic review of illicit nandrolone decanoate use describes it as a widespread class of drugs among adolescents and bodybuilders.
Clinical trials in patients have examined lean mass, bone and blood outcomes, but no controlled trial in healthy people was found among the sources reviewed. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a muscle drug said to be easier on hair and skin than testosterone, and as a possible aid to bone growth.
